name: one-media-type
title: One Media Type, Five Services
kicker: The system · why one generic client is enough
html:
One Media Type, Five Services

Five Jobs, Five Vocabularies

scm, watcher, desk, ci, env.

One Media Type

HAL with HAL Schema Forms: the data and the forms for the acts its state allows now.

No Code per Service

ARTIE knows the media type, the way a browser knows HTML.

A sixth service is a bookmark and a vocabulary, not a client.
say: Here's the part I most want you to take home. A release, for real, touches five services. A gateway in front of the forge, GitHub or GitLab. An offer watcher, which tells you when a resource starts offering an act. A release desk, where a person asks for a release. A CI service in front of a real Jenkins. And a Dev environment that a commit gets promoted to. Different jobs, different vocabularies: scm, watcher, desk, ci, env. But every one of them answers in the same media type: HAL with HAL Schema Forms, the HEART profile, application/hal+json. So ARTIE has no code for any of them. It knows the media type, the way a browser knows HTML. Notice what that means when you add a sixth service: you add a bookmark, and a vocabulary the script can name. You don't write a client. Let's walk the release through all five.

deck:ref.name: heart
deck:ref.label: HEART
deck:ref.title: HEART: one media type, information and controls together
deck:ref.summary: Hypermedia Enforced Agentic Reliable Transactions. HAL with HAL Schema Forms, plus a small profile. Every answer carries the resource's data and the forms for the acts its state allows now, each with a method, an address and a JSON Schema; an act that isn't offered can say why (hr:unavailable).

deck:ref.name: artie
deck:ref.label: ARTIE
deck:ref.title: ARTIE: the generic client
deck:ref.summary: Autonomous Restful Traversal and Interactive Engine. Coupled to HEART and HTTP, and to nothing about any one API, as a browser is to HTML. It enters by a bookmark, checks a kept script's pins against what is offered, sends each act with its If-Match validator, and caches forms and schemas (L2).

deck:ref.name: rule-3
deck:ref.label: MEDIA-TYPES
deck:ref.title: Spend the effort on media types
deck:ref.summary: In brief: describe media types and relations, not which methods go to which URIs. This is what HEART's spec is.
deck:ref.quote: “A REST API should spend almost all of its descriptive effort in defining the media type(s) used for representing resources and driving application state, or in defining extended relation names and/or hypertext-enabled mark-up for existing standard media types. Any effort spent describing what methods to use on what URIs of interest should be entirely defined within the scope of the processing rules for a media type (and, in most cases, already defined by existing media types). [Failure here implies that out-of-band information is driving interaction instead of hypertext.]”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

deck:ref.name: uniform-interface
deck:ref.label: UNIFORM-INTERFACE
deck:ref.title: Uniform interface (§5.1.5)
deck:ref.summary: One generic interface for every component; its fourth part is hypermedia as the engine of application state.
deck:ref.quote:
“The central feature that distinguishes the REST architectural style from other network-based styles is its emphasis on a uniform interface between components (Figure 5-6). By applying the software engineering principle of generality to the component interface, the overall system architecture is simplified and the visibility of interactions is improved. Implementations are decoupled from the services they provide, which encourages independent evolvability. The trade-off, though, is that a uniform interface degrades efficiency, since information is transferred in a standardized form rather than one which is specific to an application's needs. The REST interface is designed to be efficient for large-grain hypermedia data transfer, optimizing for the common case of the Web, but resulting in an interface that is not optimal for other forms of architectural interaction.

In order to obtain a uniform interface, multiple architectural constraints are needed to guide the behavior of components. REST is defined by four interface constraints: identification of resources; manipulation of resources through representations; self-descriptive messages; and, hypermedia as the engine of application state. These constraints will be discussed in Section 5.2.”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, §5.1.5

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, §5.1.5
